strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer vision problem: improving generalization when several tasks share a model. Separately aggregating loss and flatness gradients offers a plausible, broadly applicable extension to existing gradient-based multi-task methods.

The experiments cover classification and dense prediction across Multi-MNIST variants, CelebA, NYUv2, and CityScapes, using four gradient aggregation methods. Reported improvements are meaningful: F-CAGrad raises MultiFashion average accuracy from 86.51% to 87.82%, reduces CelebA error from 8.52% to 8.22%, and improves NYUv2 segmentation mIoU from 39.79 to 40.93.

The supplementary calibration results add value beyond accuracy. For example, MultiFashion average ECE decreases from 0.117 to 0.033. Perturbation sensitivity, loss landscapes, and training curves provide additional evidence consistent with the proposed motivation.

Figure 1 and Algorithm 1 make the central procedure understandable. The manuscript provides basic training details and appropriately attributes the underlying methods and datasets. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b05/review-experiment-1qiw7qxa/call-fb1b5612b0d548a99c36cfaee8ed89fd/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the distinctive contribution. Essential controls include SAM/ASAM applied to the summed task loss, direct aggregation of per-task SAM gradients, and ablations of separate loss/flatness aggregation and shared/private perturbations. Section 5.3 mainly provides diagnostics and radius sensitivity. Consequently, the results establish benefits from adding sharpness regularization, but leave the necessity and originality of the proposed decomposition insufficiently supported.

The theoretical connection to Algorithm 1 is incomplete. Theorem 1 bounds losses under joint perturbations of shared and private parameters, whereas the algorithm evaluates these perturbations separately. Moreover, adding independently aggregated loss and flatness directions does not generally preserve common descent for the resulting task objectives. The per-task generalization bounds therefore do not establish the claimed behavior of the actual update.

The formal bound also needs substantive clarification. Appendix A bounds Gaussian-tail loss contributions using tail probabilities, which requires a bounded-loss assumption that is absent from the theorem statements. The simultaneous guarantee leaves the relationship between the confidence parameters ξ, δ, and task count insufficiently specified. These issues affect the stated guarantee and its applicability, although repairing them would not by itself validate the proposed aggregation rule.

The implementation description does not fully match the experiments: Algorithm 1 specifies Euclidean SAM perturbations, while Appendix B.2 states that adaptive SAM is used. The corresponding adaptive update is not provided. Selected perturbation radii and the validation protocol for the extensive 0.005–5 search are also missing, and the supplied manuscript gives no URL for its claimed public implementation.

Practical costs and statistical uncertainty are incompletely evaluated. Task-specific perturbed evaluations can substantially increase training cost, especially for 40-task CelebA, yet no runtime, memory, or equal-compute comparisons are reported. Tables 2–4 omit variability estimates, limiting confidence in small differences between methods.

Claims about benefiting all tasks need qualification. The paper acknowledges that F-MGDA reduces NYUv2 segmentation mIoU from 30.47 to 26.42 despite improving the aggregate score; this is a legitimate trade-off that should also temper the broader claims. Furthermore, the low-resource and noisy-label motivations are not directly tested: the reported noise experiments concern parameter perturbations.
